stations.challenge: Put these in order: freedom, money, friends, fame and a job you enjoy. Explain your first choice.
followUpQuestions: Can you succeed without earning much money?
Who influences your idea of success?
Has your definition changed as you have grown up?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: How would you describe a successful life?
stations.stretch: Imagine nobody knew about your successes. Would anything change? Why?
stations.subtitle: Start by asking what we are really aiming for.
stations.title: What Counts as Success?

stations.challenge: Compare a student who gets excellent marks but hardly sleeps with one who learns slowly but enjoys school.
followUpQuestions: What important abilities do grades miss?
When do grades motivate students?
Should schools reward effort as well as results?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: Do good grades show how capable a student is?
stations.stretch: Design one fairer way to give feedback at school.
stations.subtitle: When achievements become numbers.
stations.title: The Grade Trap

stations.challenge: Your parents offer to pay for university only if they can choose your subject. Negotiate.
followUpQuestions: Why do parents sometimes prefer safe careers?
How can teenagers disagree politely?
When is compromise a good idea?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: How much should family expectations influence your plans?
stations.stretch: Suggest a compromise that respects both independence and responsibility.
stations.subtitle: Expectations from family and other people.
stations.title: Whose Dream Is It?

stations.challenge: Imagine you see online that a friend has won an important competition. How do you feel? Why?
followUpQuestions: Why do we compare our lives online?
What does social media leave out?
How can we notice our own progress?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: Does comparing yourself with others help you improve?
stations.stretch: Invent two habits that make social comparison less harmful.
stations.subtitle: Why does everybody else seem ahead?
stations.title: The Comparison Trap

stations.challenge: A talented student never enters competitions because she is afraid of losing. Give her realistic advice.
followUpQuestions: What can you learn from a mistake?
Why are some students afraid to try?
What could a supportive teacher say?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.stretch: Discuss when it makes sense to stop trying rather than continue.
stations.subtitle: Mistakes, risk and trying again.
stations.title: The Fear of Failure

stations.challenge: A student sleeps only five hours a night because of clubs and homework. Give them practical advice.
followUpQuestions: Why do some students feel guilty when resting?
How can you recognise too much stress?
What is a healthy weekly routine?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: Is being constantly busy a sign of success?
stations.stretch: Propose a school rule that protects students’ well-being.
stations.subtitle: Ambition, rest and stress.
stations.title: Always Busy, Never Enough

stations.challenge: Choose: an interesting job with low pay or a safe but boring job. Explain your choice.
followUpQuestions: What makes a career meaningful?
How much job security do you need?
Could a boring job support a happy life?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: Should job satisfaction matter more than salary?
stations.stretch: Describe a third choice and its limitations.
stations.subtitle: Choosing a future without perfect options.
stations.title: Passion or Money?

stations.challenge: Write a three-line ‘success manifesto’: We refuse to… / We value… / We remember…
followUpQuestions: Who decides what makes a life impressive?
Can you be ambitious and happy with your life at the same time?
Which social expectation would you challenge?
languageSupport: Do you agree, or do you see it differently?
stations.mainQuestion: Is it enough to be an ordinary, happy person?
stations.stretch: Challenge one unrealistic idea about success in your society.
stations.subtitle: Do we really have to stand out?
stations.title: The Right to Be Ordinary

toolkit.example: I believe that … / Personally, I’d say …
The main reason is … / For instance, …
I see your point, but … / That’s true to some extent.
Could you explain why? / Can you give an example?

vocabulary.explanation: something important you manage to do
the reason why you want to do something
a good mix of work and personal time
a series of jobs in your working life
a strong wish to achieve something
an agreement where both sides give something up
attention or praise for what you do

warmUp.note: If you want: a short activity to start.
warmUp.prompt: Choose three things that matter most to teenagers. Agree on a joint top three.

ui.lessonGoal: Express opinions, explain reasons and ask follow-up questions.
ui.levelTip: Choose about 5 stations. Give a reason for each answer and ask one follow-up question.

presentation.introduction: Grades. Expectations. Competition. Failure. The future. Who decides what success should look like? Explore the question together, one conversation at a time.
presentation.privacyNotice: You can use fictional examples. Nobody needs to share personal grades, family problems or private experiences.
quickStart: Give a reason or an example.
Ask your partner a follow-up question.
Open the challenge if you need more to discuss.
presentation.subtitle: A conversation, not a test
